name: Apple cider vinegar rinse
lead: An apple cider vinegar (ACV) rinse is a home hair treatment in which diluted apple cider vinegar is poured over the hair and scalp after washing. People use it to leave hair smoother, shinier and less greasy-feeling without a commercial product: the acidity is said to flatten the hair cuticle, remove residue and bring the scalp toward its natural pH, so hair reflects more light and tangles less.

Apple cider vinegar is roughly 94 percent water and 5 percent acetic acid, according to Wikipedia, which describes clinical evidence for its health uses as poor and notes that regulators and major health organizations do not recommend it for any therapeutic use [1]. A 2025 literature review in the journal Cutis described the ACV rinse method, in the context of synthetic hair extensions, as an anecdotal remedy lacking data to support it [2]. No controlled trials of ACV rinses on natural hair were found.

The rinse is a common companion to the "no poo" approach to hair washing, in which people wash with water, baking soda or other non-shampoo products and finish with a diluted acid such as apple vinegar.[6] Medical News Today reports that the scalp's ideal pH is about 5.5 and that support for vinegar lowering it is mostly anecdotal; published trials of vinegar rinses on hair were not found.[7]

paras: Apple cider vinegar is made by fermenting apple juice, first to ethanol by yeast and then to acetic acid by Acetobacter bacteria, and unfiltered versions may contain a cellulose-rich biofilm called the mother [1]. Hair-rinse use applies diluted vinegar after shampooing; Wikipedia's vinegar article does not mention hair or other cosmetic uses [1].

The practice has a long folk-remedy history alongside oils and herbal rinses, and it is currently discussed in hair-care circles as a low-cost step costing little more than a bottle of vinegar. Typical accounts describe it as an occasional step after washing, used for greasiness, residue or dullness, with frequency varying by person.

Proponents say the acidity removes residue, flattens the cuticle, adds shine and helps the scalp. Wikipedia reports that acidic shampoos in the pH 4 to 6 range are the most common type because they do not swell the hair shaft [3], and the hair conditioner article lists acidifiers such as citric acid as ingredients that lower hair's net negative charge and reduce frizz [4]. Neither source tests vinegar rinses.

Wikipedia notes that sebum builds up on a typical adult scalp roughly every two to three days and that hair-shaft damage cannot be repaired biologically, so conditioning products work on the surface of the fibre.[3][4] Medical News Today states that the scalp's ideal pH is about 5.5 and that many shampoos are higher; it says the case that vinegar lowers scalp pH rests mostly on personal anecdotes.[7]

Wikipedia describes the no poo movement as ranging from water-only washing to using baking soda followed by a diluted acid rinse such as apple vinegar. Advocates argue that shampoo is an unnecessary expense and that stripping sebum prompts more oil production, a cycle they say takes up to six weeks to break; these are described as proponents' arguments rather than established findings. In 2007, Australian radio presenter Richard Glover challenged listeners to go six weeks without shampoo, and of more than 500 participants, 86 percent reported their hair was either better or the same.[6] Wikipedia notes that synthetic shampoos appeared in the 1930s and that daily shampooing became the US norm in the 1970s and 1980s.[6]

Wikipedia lists reported harms of apple cider vinegar including skin burns from topical use for skin conditions, eye irritation and possible corneal injury, and allergic reactions in people allergic to apples, and notes that acid levels vary between brands [1]. Grokipedia describes a case of second-degree burns in a child from vinegar-soaked cotton balls left on overnight and says undiluted vinegar can cause chemical burns with prolonged contact [5].

Medical News Today reports a 2012 case of an 8-year-old with Crohn's disease who sustained chemical burns from undiluted vinegar-soaked cotton balls left on lesions for about 8 hours, and cites the National Eczema Association as warning that large amounts may damage the mouth, teeth, throat and stomach.[7]

No studies found of ACV rinses on natural hair. A 2025 literature review in Cutis addressed the ACV rinse method for synthetic hair extensions and characterised it as an anecdotal remedy without validating data [2].

A 2019 study in Pediatric Dermatology, as summarised by Medical News Today, had participants with atopic dermatitis and controls soak one forearm in diluted vinegar (0.5 percent acetic acid) and the other in water for 10 minutes; skin pH fell and stayed low for 15 minutes in the atopic dermatitis group and 60 minutes in controls, increased water loss was seen in both groups, and most participants with atopic dermatitis had mild to moderate irritation. The researchers concluded the effect was temporary. This study examined forearm skin, not scalp or hair.[7] Medical News Today also reports that undiluted ACV showed strong antimicrobial activity in a 2019 laboratory study, with weaker antifungal activity at lower concentrations, and that high-quality research has not confirmed ACV for dandruff.[7]

lore.intro: ACV rinses are mentioned in hair-care and no-poo threads on T Nation as an occasional step used instead of or after washing.[8][9]

claims.claim: An ACV rinse can stand in for shampoo or clean oily hair
claims.believers: One T Nation poster describes having stopped shampooing and rinsing with water, with a quick ACV rinse about once a month when the hair feels greasy.[8] Another thread recommends following a scalp wash with an ACV rinse.[9]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the no poo movement's claims as proponents' arguments rather than established findings, and no published trial tests vinegar rinses against shampoo.[6]

claims.claim: The acidity lowers scalp pH and flattens the cuticle for shine
claims.believers: Proponents say an acid rinse closes the cuticle and leaves hair smoother and shinier.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that acidic shampoos (pH 4 to 6) are most common because they do not swell the hair shaft, and conditioners may use acidifiers to reduce frizz; a forearm study found vinegar lowered skin pH only temporarily.[3][4][7]

claims.claim: Vinegar is harmless because it is natural
claims.believers: Users describe it as a cheap, gentle kitchen product.
claims.experts: Wikipedia and case reports describe burns from undiluted use and eye irritation, and a Cutis review calls the ACV rinse an anecdotal remedy lacking validating data for synthetic-extension use.[1][2][7]

card.summary: A diluted vinegar rinse after shampooing, said to clarify and add shine; supported only by anecdote, with burn and irritation reports for strong vinegar.
card.note: Undiluted vinegar has caused chemical burns; eye contact is a documented hazard.

quick.overview:
An ACV rinse is diluted apple cider vinegar poured over hair after washing. People who use it say it removes buildup and makes hair shinier and smoother.

A 2025 review in Cutis called the method an anecdotal remedy lacking supporting data, and no trials on natural hair were found.
quick.mechanism: The theory is that the acetic acid, about 5 percent of the vinegar, lowers the pH of the hair surface, which proponents say flattens the cuticle and dissolves residue. Studies of vinegar rinses specifically have not been published.
quick.risks: Vinegar is acidic. Wikipedia lists eye irritation, possible corneal injury and skin burns with topical use, and product labels advise dilution. Allergy is possible in people allergic to apples.
